wine.name: Eroica Riesling
wine.grapes: Riesling, drawn from several vineyards in the desert east of the Cascades.
wine.sites: Columbia Valley vineyards east of the Cascades: the early vintages drew mostly on the warm Cold Creek Vineyard, later ones more on cooler sites.
wine.making: Fermented cool, so that the fruit and the acidity stay bright, and raised for some months, chiefly in stainless steel tanks. The wine is bottled with a little sugar left in it, enough to make it off dry against its high acidity.
wine.glass: Lime, green apple and white peach over orange blossom and a wet stone note; light in body and off dry, the touch of sweetness held in check by bright, high acidity, with a long, juicy finish.
wine.ageing: Bright and ready at once and at its freshest within a few years, though a good vintage keeps beyond ten years, gaining honey and the petrol note of aged Riesling.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass, with crab, pork or a spiced dish from Asia.

label.means: The wine's name, taken from the Eroica, the Third Symphony of Beethoven.
The Mosel estate of Bernkastel that makes this Riesling together with Chateau Ste. Michelle.
The broad appellation of the desert east of the Cascades, which lets the partners blend several vineyards.

records.table: Eroica is the Riesling Chateau Ste. Michelle has made since 1999 with Dr. Loosen of the Mosel: Columbia Valley fruit, fermented cool in steel and left off dry, with lime, white peach and a wet stone note. Pour it well chilled beside crab or a spiced dish.
records.story: Chateau Ste. Michelle grew out of the end of Prohibition. By the company's account, two Seattle firms, Pommerelle and the National Wine Company, began making fruit wines in 1934, and by the mid 1950s the two had joined as American Wine Growers, a maker of mostly sweet, fortified wines. In 1967 the company launched Ste. Michelle Vintners for wines named by their grape, a Cabernet Sauvignon, a Pinot Noir, a Semillon and a Grenache rosé, and retained André Tchelistcheff (1901 to 1994), the Russian born winemaker of Napa's Beaulieu, as its consultant. In 1972 it began planting Cold Creek Vineyard in the desert east of the Cascades. In 1974 its 1972 Riesling came first in a blind tasting held by the Los Angeles Times, and Riesling became the grape the house is known by. In 1976 it moved into a French style château at Woodinville, near Seattle, built on a lumber baron's estate of 1912, and took the name Chateau Ste. Michelle. In 1999 Chateau Ste. Michelle and the Mosel estate Dr. Loosen began a Riesling made together from Washington grapes, and the first Eroica followed that year, named after the Third Symphony of Ludwig van Beethoven (1770 to 1827). Eroica ties the Mosel to the Columbia Valley: Riesling in the German manner, grown in the Washington desert.

others.name: Eroica Ice Wine
others.note: A sweet Riesling of the same partnership, from grapes frozen on the vine and pressed while frozen.

others.name: Cold Creek Vineyard Cabernet Sauvignon
others.note: Cabernet from the desert vineyard the company began planting in 1972, a planting that by the company's account doubled Washington's plantings of wine grapes.

traps: Chateau Ste. Michelle's winery and château stand at Woodinville, west of the Cascades, but the grapes for Eroica grow in the desert east of the mountains.
Eroica is the partnership with Dr. Loosen of the Mosel; Col Solare is a separate Red Mountain partnership with the Antinori family of Tuscany.
Eroica Riesling is off dry, neither a dry Riesling nor a dessert wine; the Eroica Ice Wine is the sweet one.

wine.name: Quilceda Creek Cabernet Sauvignon
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, all or nearly all of it, with a little Merlot in some years.
wine.sites: Above all Champoux Vineyard in the Horse Heaven Hills, first planted in 1972, with the family's own Mach One vineyard and, in some years, Red Mountain fruit from Klipsun and Tapteil.
wine.making: The Cabernet is aged in French oak barrels, all or nearly all of them new, for about twenty to twenty two months, as the house's own notes on its vintages record, and is then bottled.
wine.glass: Ripe and dense yet smooth, with no green edge: cassis, blackberry and black cherry over cedar, cocoa and graphite, held by fine, polished tannin and fresh acidity through a long finish.
wine.ageing: Dense but already approachable young; the house reckons that the wine of a strong year takes some twenty to twenty five years to reach its peak.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; give a young bottle an hour or two in a decanter, and pour an old one gently off its sediment; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: Wide enough to hold Champoux and the house's other vineyards under one name.
The grape named on the label; United States law asks that at least three quarters of the wine be that grape.

records.table: A family house at Snohomish, north of Seattle, Quilceda Creek draws its Cabernet Sauvignon above all from Champoux Vineyard in the Horse Heaven Hills. New French oak frames its cassis and graphite, ripe and smooth, with polished tannin.
records.story: Quilceda Creek's roots run back to Napa. Its founder was a nephew, on his mother's side, of André Tchelistcheff (1901 to 1994), who shaped Beaulieu's Cabernet, and by the house's account the uncle guided the family at the start. In 1978 the nephew and his wife established the winery at Snohomish, by the house's count the twelfth bonded in Washington since Prohibition, and in 1979 he made its first vintage, a Cabernet Sauvignon, in the family garage. In 1986 the house began buying grapes from the Mercer vineyard in the Horse Heaven Hills, first planted in 1972 and later known as Champoux. In 1996 the Champoux family and a small group of wineries that had long bought its fruit, Quilceda among them, formed a company to own the vineyard, and Quilceda took its first share in 1997. In the early 2000s the founder's son oversaw the planting of the family's Galitzine vineyard on Red Mountain, its vines set close and dense. From the 2009 vintage the house's second wine, made from younger vines and from barrels set aside from the Cabernet, took the name CVR. The house has kept to Cabernet Sauvignon above all, and its wine carries Tchelistcheff's Napa east of the Cascades.

others.name: Quilceda Creek CVR Columbia Valley Red Wine
others.note: The second wine, from younger vines and barrels set aside from the Cabernet, called CVR from the 2009 vintage; the house expects it to peak far sooner.

others.name: Galitzine Vineyard Cabernet Sauvignon
others.note: Cabernet from the family's own vineyard on Red Mountain, planted close in the early 2000s, named for the family and first released with the 2004 vintage.

traps: Snohomish, north of Seattle, is where Quilceda Creek makes its wine, not where its grapes grow: those come from east of the Cascades, above all from Champoux.
CVR is Quilceda Creek's second wine, Columbia Valley Red, not a reserve or a vineyard bottling of the Cabernet.
Champoux Vineyard was first planted in 1972 as the Mercer vineyard; Champoux is the name of the family who later ran it, not of a winery.

wine.name: Leonetti Cabernet Sauvignon
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, the great majority, with small parts of Malbec, Petit Verdot or Cabernet Franc in some years.
wine.sites: Vineyards across the Walla Walla Valley: Mill Creek Upland, Loess and Seven Hills in the 2000s, later also Holy Roller, the Leonetti Old Block and Serra Pedace, a steep, east facing hillside of shallow, rocky soil first planted in 2010.
wine.making: Aged for about twenty two months in oak. Earlier vintages mixed French barrels with American, Hungarian and other oak; later ones use French barrels and puncheons, some new and some filled once before, beside large, neutral oval casks, or botti.
wine.glass: Black cherry, cassis and plum wrapped in cocoa, cedar and clove; full and plush, its ripe, supple tannin lifted by fresh acidity into a long, polished finish.
wine.ageing: Generous and supple on release, yet the house says it makes the wine to age for twenty to thirty years in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two and an old one only to leave the sediment behind; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The house, named for the founder's grandparents, who came from Calabria and, by the family's account, farmed in Walla Walla from 1906.
The appellation of 1984 inside the Columbia Valley, crossing into Oregon; printed on this Cabernet from the 1999 vintage.

records.table: The modern Walla Walla Valley had no commercial winery before Leonetti Cellar, bonded in 1977. Its Cabernet Sauvignon, drawn from vineyards across the valley, is plush and ripe, with supple tannin under black cherry, cocoa and cedar.
records.story: The house takes its name from a Calabrian family. The founder's grandparents came to Walla Walla from the village of Serra Pedace and, by the house's account, set up their farm there in 1906. In 1974 their grandson planted Cabernet Sauvignon and Riesling on the family land, on the hillside above the old homestead. He and his wife bonded Leonetti Cellar in 1977 as the first commercial winery of the modern Walla Walla Valley, and its first vintage, 1978, gave a Riesling and the house's first Cabernet Sauvignon. Woodward Canyon followed in 1981, and in December 1982 that 1978 Cabernet took first place in a national tasting held by a wine buying guide, the news that put Washington red wine before the whole country. The Walla Walla Valley became an appellation in 1984, and the Cabernet came to draw on vineyards across it, among them a steep, east facing hillside of shallow, rocky soil that the house named Serra Pedace after the grandparents' village. Leonetti is where the modern wine of the Walla Walla Valley begins, and its Cabernet is the bottle that made the valley's name.

The Walla Walla Valley appellation crosses into Oregon; Leonetti Cellar's winery stands on the Washington side, at Walla Walla.

report: Searches for this record: five, four restricted to leonetticellar.com, and one on the Walla Walla Valley Wine Alliance's site shared with Woodward Canyon; no source met gave how the Cabernet is fermented, so the making speaks only of its ageing.
The house's first label, by its own photograph caption, was a White Riesling of 1978; no source met confirmed a Cabernet of 1978, so the record does not claim one.

The library calls Leonetti the first winery in the Walla Walla Valley, but vines were planted and wine made in the valley from the 1850s (the Walla Walla Valley Wine Alliance, the Wine Commission), so the record says the first commercial winery of the modern valley, as the region's own body does.
The library's style line of generous new oak fits the older vintages; the house's sheets for 2019 to 2022 give French barrels and puncheons, new and once used, with neutral oval botti.
The grandparents are not named, for want of their dates; the house's pages call them Francesco and Rosa, Francesco and Rosalina, and Frank and Rose.

The 1974 planting above the homestead is told on the house's family page; whether it is the Leonetti Old Block, whose Merlot the house dates to 1976, is not settled, so the record does not join them; the house's sheets label the Cabernet Columbia Valley in 1995 and 1997, American in 1996 and Walla Walla Valley from 1999, a history left out of the story for want of room.
Woodward Canyon of 1981 and the appellation of 1984 in the story rest on the library's region record and the Walla Walla Valley Wine Alliance's fact sheet.
The respelling lee-oh-NET-ee follows the family's American usage as heard, not a source, and should be confirmed.

wine.name: Woodward Canyon Old Vines Cabernet Sauvignon
wine.grapes: Mostly Cabernet Sauvignon, with a little Petit Verdot and Malbec in some years.
wine.sites: Old Cabernet blocks, chiefly Champoux in the Horse Heaven Hills, planted from 1972, with its Block One, and Sagemoor north of Pasco, with Weinbau and the estate vineyard at Lowden in some vintages.
wine.making: As the house's notes describe it, the grapes are picked by hand and sorted, given a cold soak of about two days, then fermented in small stainless steel fermenters; the malolactic fermentation starts on its own, and the wine is aged for about twenty one months in new French oak barrels.
wine.glass: Blackcurrant, black plum and blueberry against graphite, cedar and dried herbs, with a savoury edge of tomato leaf; dark and firm rather than plush, with fine grained tannin and brisk acidity.
wine.ageing: Firm and closed when young, it needs eight to ten years in a strong vintage and then holds for twenty or more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; a young bottle wants an hour or two of air in a decanter, and an old one should be poured off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: Fruit from old Cabernet blocks, chiefly at Champoux, whose vines go back to 1972, and at Sagemoor.
The state appellation printed on later labels; the old blocks behind the wine lie outside the Walla Walla Valley.

records.table: Woodward Canyon's Old Vines Cabernet Sauvignon is grown outside the Walla Walla Valley, on old blocks at Champoux and Sagemoor, though the winery, bonded at Lowden in 1981, was the valley's second of the modern era. Dark, savoury and firm, it rewards patience.
records.story: At Lowden, west of Walla Walla, the founder planted his first vines on the family farm in the 1970s, Chardonnay first. Woodward Canyon Winery followed there in 1981, bonded by the founder and his wife as the second winery of the modern Walla Walla Valley, after Leonetti Cellar of 1977, and the couple helped win federal approval for the Walla Walla Valley appellation, granted in 1984. The Cabernet called Old Vines began with the winery in 1981 as the Dedication Series, and for its first twenty five years each label honoured a different pioneer of the Walla Walla Valley. The house built the wine on Cabernet from old blocks outside the valley: Sagemoor, north of Pasco, and Champoux in the Horse Heaven Hills, set out in 1972 under another name, which, the house says, hold some of the oldest Cabernet in Washington. Champoux's original Block One became a mainstay of the wine, and in 1996 Woodward Canyon was among the wineries that became part owners of that vineyard with the Champoux family. In time the house added a second Cabernet line, the Artist Series, and a separate Estate Old Vines from the oldest block of its own vineyard at Lowden. Old Vines remains the house's founding Cabernet, dark and savoury, a counterpoint to the plusher Walla Walla wines that came after it.

others.name: Artist Series Cabernet Sauvignon
others.note: Made since 1992 and blended from several Washington vineyards; the house itself calls it its flagship, though Old Vines is the older Cabernet.

others.name: Estate Old Vines Cabernet Sauvignon
others.note: A separate wine, all Cabernet from the oldest block of the estate vineyard at Lowden, fermented with the estate's native yeast.

traps: Woodward Canyon came second among the wineries of the modern Walla Walla Valley, in 1981, four years after Leonetti Cellar; it was never the first.
Old Vines Cabernet Sauvignon draws on old blocks across the Columbia Valley, chiefly Champoux and Sagemoor; the Estate Old Vines is a different wine, from the oldest block at Lowden.
Woodward Canyon is a winery, neither a vineyard nor an appellation.

records.place: Milton-Freewater, The Rocks District, Walla Walla Valley, Oregon

wine.name: Bionic Frog Syrah
wine.grapes: Syrah alone or almost alone, from the one vineyard.
wine.sites: Coccinelle, a vineyard planted in 1998 on the basalt cobbles of The Rocks District, on the Oregon side of the Walla Walla Valley; coccinelle is French for ladybird.
wine.making: The vineyard is farmed biodynamically. The grapes ferment on their native yeasts in concrete tanks, with a large share of whole bunches, a share that has grown over the years, and the wine is then aged for some eighteen to twenty one months in French oak, in barrels and larger casks, with little or no new wood.
wine.glass: Blackberry and violet under smoked meat, black olive brine, iron and a bloody, savoury note; full yet silky, with fine tannin, fresh acidity and a wild, persistent close.
wine.ageing: It drinks openly and generously at first, then gains savour over ten years or more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; an hour in a decanter for a young bottle; a large, wide bowled red wine glass.

label.means: The name of the house's Syrah from the Coccinelle vineyard, first made with the 2000 vintage.
The appellation on the label: it crosses the state line, and this vineyard lies on its Oregon side.

records.table: On the basalt cobbles of Milton-Freewater, on the Oregon side of the Walla Walla Valley, Cayuse Vineyards farms Coccinelle biodynamically, and Bionic Frog is its Syrah. Smoked meat, olive brine and iron come before the blackberry and violet.
records.story: A field of stones set Cayuse in motion. In 1996 a young Frenchman from a Champagne family, in Walla Walla at the time, was driving with a friend on the Oregon side of the valley when he saw open ground littered with stones the size of softballs. As the house tells the story, he dropped his plan to settle in the Willamette Valley and resolved to buy the land and plant it. The stones are rounded basalt laid down by the Walla Walla River, and they put him in mind of Châteauneuf-du-Pape. In 1997 he planted Cailloux, his first vineyard in the stones. Its first Syrah, of 1998, was sold as Cobblestone Vineyard and renamed Cailloux with the 1999 vintage. Coccinelle followed in 1998, and its Syrah, labelled Bionic Frog, began with the 2000 vintage. In 2002 the house began to farm biodynamically, by its own account the first estate in the Walla Walla Valley to do so in full. In 2015 the cobbled fan became an appellation of its own, The Rocks District of Milton-Freewater, wholly in Oregon and inside the Walla Walla Valley. Bionic Frog puts the taste of that ground on a wine list: Syrah that is savoury before it is fruity.

The cobbles of the Rocks District are basalt laid down by the Walla Walla River, not the quartzite galets of Châteauneuf-du-Pape.

report: Searches for this record: seven, one restricted to cayusevineyards.com; one search for the meaning of the name Bionic Frog found nothing, and the ageing in French oak of which only a small part is new rests on Skurnik's listing and on Bibendum's, which also speaks of large old foudres.
The name Bionic Frog, by one quoted account a nickname the founder's fellow cellar workers gave him, and the Cayuse name's link to the French cailloux, each rest on one source and are left out.

Native yeasts and concrete tanks stand in Vinous, Wine Spectator and Rare Wine Co for the house's Syrahs; that Bionic Frog moved from stainless steel to concrete with the 2006 vintage is in Vinous alone and is left out, and the whole bunch share is given only as large, since the sources give a quarter in the early years and three quarters or more later.

The library says the winery and the trade are in Walla Walla, Washington; Good Fruit Grower reported in 2015 that the house had built a winemaking facility on the Oregon side, inside the Rocks District, so the record says nothing of where the wine is made.

Why the label says Walla Walla Valley rather than The Rocks District is not argued: the rule that a wine be finished in a state the appellation touches was met with a TTB proposal of 2015 to change it, whose outcome was not found.
The 2015 date of the Rocks District rests on the library's region record and Good Fruit Grower; the founder's Champagne family on the library's producer record.
Coccinelle's planting in 1998 rests on Skurnik's listing and Vinous; a Decanter page met in search says Coccinelle holds Roussanne as well as Syrah, so the grapes say all or nearly all Syrah.
